A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same particle-tracking framework and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained material can be matched reliably despite new sections and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulated tracking experiments, training curves, loss-landscape analyses, model-similarity measurements and connectivity results, including appendix analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds hit-graph versus line-graph experiments, graph-size measurements and computational benchmarks in Appendix D.

M1.justification: The proposed line-graph construction, interaction network, layer-wise assignment solver, blackbox differentiation and PAT/PTT losses remain unchanged. Expanded explanations clarify the procedure; the added hit-graph architecture is an evaluated comparator.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same simulated Bergen pCT tracking task with 100, 150 and 200 mm water phantoms and 50, 100 and 150 primaries per frame. The corrected Table 1 caption matches settings already used in v1. Downstream reconstruction and simulation-to-reality studies remain future work.

E2.justification: Appendix D adds a conventional hit-graph interaction-network comparator based on DeZoort et al., evaluated under PTT and all three PAT configurations. This supplies a substantial direct comparison for the proposed graph representation, beyond the retained track-follower and RL comparisons in Table 1.

E3.justification: The original experiment settings remain intact. The added hit-graph study uses hidden dimension 64 versus 16 for the line graph, and introduces FLOP and separate prediction/full-reconstruction timing measurements. Figure 10 spans 30,000 training steps, although the general methods still specify 10,000, leaving the new study's budget incompletely reconciled.

E4.justification: New Appendix D tests whether the line-graph representation improves convergence and reconstruction, and examines its graph-size and computational costs. Tables 5–6 and Figures 10–12 add a substantial architectural ablation and efficiency analysis. Existing loss-landscape, filtering and similarity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 specifies ten timing evaluations per test frame for the new runtime benchmark. The original five independently initialized networks and Welch's t-tests remain unchanged; the statistical-testing appendix moves from F to G without a new testing procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their numerical results, but Appendix D adds substantial results. For example, at 100 primaries/frame and a 100 mm phantom, Table 6 reports PAT lambda=25 purity of 53.5±3.8% for the new hit-graph comparator versus the retained line-graph result of 87.3±0.2%. New graph-size, convergence, FLOP and timing results are also reported; these are additional comparisons, not improvements to the retained model.

T1.justification: The mathematical framework, assumptions and loss/connectivity definitions are retained. Equation 12 clarifies argmin and assignment notation already expressed in v1's solver discussion, without changing the optimization problem or adding a substantive derivation or proof.

C1.justification: The central contributions and claims about differentiable tracking, competitive reconstruction, connected minima and prediction instability remain. Section 6 newly makes the tradeoff between faster convergence at larger lambda and reduced robustness an explicit concluding claim, refining the earlier recommendation for smaller lambda.

C2.justification: v2 adds specific interpretations concerning possible effects on pCT contrast and spatial resolution, persistent hardware nondeterminism, and the informativeness of gradients at larger lambda. It explicitly qualifies connectivity as indirect evidence for downstream optimization. Appendix D also interprets the representation's accuracy, parameter-efficiency and runtime tradeoffs.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new comparator's features and hidden dimension, NVIDIA A100 timing hardware and fvcore FLOP tool, and explicitly states that filter thresholds remain fixed during evaluation. Conversely, replacing the detector-geometry diagram removes its detailed material specifications. Existing hyperparameters, loss-analysis implementation details and resource-access statements are retained.

R1.justification: New Section 3.2 substantially expands positioning around coupled ML pipelines, error propagation and modular versus end-to-end optimization, drawing on Sculley, Nushi, Modi, Yu and Hilprecht, among others. The introduction and related work also distinguish recent tracking approaches by Stroud and Reuter that combine tracking with parameter estimation.

P1.justification: The introduction and method explanations are expanded, a pipeline-background subsection and explicit interpretation paragraphs are added, and terminology and notation are clarified. The overall six-section narrative and most existing passages remain, with appendix renumbering following the new ablation.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces the detector-material diagram with a track-combinatorics schematic. v2 adds Tables 5–6 and Figures 10–12, annotates Figure 8 with selected thresholds and error rates, and redisplays retained scores alongside new comparator results. Existing figures and tables are also relocated within the publication layout.

improvement.justification: Appendix D provides useful evidence for the previously untested line-graph design choice and exposes its runtime cost, while Sections 5.3–5.4 clarify the limits of downstream implications. These gains are tempered by inconsistent FLOP reporting—Figure 11 labels the hit graph as more expensive while the prose says the reverse—and the unresolved training-budget description. The main empirical findings remain unchanged.
